title: ME03a: When Growth Becomes a Trap
author: Richard Claydon
summary: Claydon tells the story of Maya, a senior leader who did all the right developmental work and ended up feeling that growth itself had become a performance. She finds hope in adult development theory such as Kegan's stages, but sees the upper rungs turn into another ladder and an inhuman ideal. Organisations built around higher consciousness fare no better, because developmental language can shield power from critique and becomes unfalsifiable without checks and feedback loops. The essay's move is to replace vertical ascent with horizontal coherence, locating leadership in high-quality connection between people rather than in an evolved self. It closes with reflection prompts on self, role and system. Useful as a corrective to leadership-development culture that treats maturity as a badge.
points: Developmental stage models can slide into virtue performance dressed as growth, turning self-improvement into another status ladder.
Developmental vocabulary used inside organisations can become a diagnosis that shuts down dissent ("you haven't reached the next stage yet") and is unfalsifiable without structural checks.
Claydon, drawing on Becky Andree's work on high-quality connections, relocates leadership in small relational moments between people rather than in individual cognition.
The proposed shift is from vertical ladders to horizontal coherence, from self-transcendence to mutual presence, and from performing maturity to practising connection.
The closing SELF, ROLE and SYSTEM questions give leaders a concrete way to audit what they are performing in the name of growth.
quotes: But the more she tried to reach for it, the more it felt like chasing smoke. The ideal leader started to sound inhuman: always reflective, never reactive; always curious, never constrained; always able to act with wisdom, no matter how incoherent the system. That didn’t feel developmental. That felt performative again—just with more spiritual vocabulary.

She’d seen it before. Teams where power was invisible, but still present. Cultures that preached trust but punished dissent. Leadership circles where developmental language became a shield against critique. Where disagreement was met not with engagement, but with diagnosis. You just haven’t reached the next stage yet.

It wasn’t that the systems were fake. Some were sincerely trying. But many of the models she encountered lacked one crucial thing: a structural immune system. No checks. No feedback loops. Just vibes and vocabulary. And that made the developmental language dangerous. Not because it was wrong. But because it became unfalsifiable.

That’s when she found Becky Andree’s work on high-quality connections. The idea that leadership isn’t just about cognition or strategy—but about relational energy. Micro-interactions that create trust, resonance, and possibility. Not mystical. Not heroic. Just real.

What Maya realised—and what I suspect many of us are realising—is that real growth isn’t a ladder. It’s a capacity. To stay present. To hold tension. To perform a role with some kind of integrity in the middle of a system that won’t stabilise. That doesn’t make you “transformed.” It makes you tired. But also trustworthy.

The trouble with becoming is that it never ends. And when we turn development into doctrine—when we measure maturity by who can speak the language of paradox while still hitting quarterly targets—we lose the point entirely.
Growth isn’t about escaping the mess. It’s about becoming someone who can stay in it—without being undone.
